paragraphs.text: VII. AGAINST FELIX, IN TWO BOOKS
BOOK ONE

In the sixth consulship of Honorius Augustus, on the seventh day before the Ides of December, AUGUSTINE, bishop of the Catholic Church of the district of Hippo Regius, said: You know that yesterday you said you could defend the scriptures of Mani and maintain that they contain the truth. If you are willing to do this today too, or if you are confident that you can, say so.
FELIX the Manichaean said: I do not deny that I said I would defend my law, if the authors of my law were brought forward here before us.

And when Bishop Augustine had brought out the letter of Mani that they call the Letter of the Foundation, he said: If I read from this book, which you see me holding, the letter of Mani that you call the Letter of the Foundation, can you recognize whether it is the genuine letter?
FELIX said: I recognize it.
AUGUSTINE said: Take it and read it yourself.

And when Felix had taken the book, he read: "Mani, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the providence of God the Father. These are words of salvation from the everlasting and living fountain. Whoever hears them and first believes them, and then keeps what they teach, will never be subject to death but will enjoy eternal and glorious life. For surely he must be judged blessed who has been instructed in this divine knowledge, by which he is set free and will abide in everlasting life." Bishop AUGUSTINE said: You have certainly recognized the letter of your Mani?
FELIX said: I have recognized it.

AUGUSTINE said: Then prove to us how this Mani is an apostle of Jesus Christ. For we never read of him among the apostles in the gospel. We know who was ordained in the place of Judas the betrayer, namely Saint Matthias; and everyone recognizes who was called afterward by the voice of the Lord from heaven, namely Paul the apostle. So prove to us that this Mani is an apostle of Christ, as he dared to put at the head of his letter.

FELIX said: And let Your Holiness prove to me what is written in the gospel, where Christ says: "I am going to the Father, and I am sending you the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who will lead you into all truth." Prove to me that some writing other than this one is the writing of the Holy Spirit whom Christ promised, in which all truth is to be found. If I find the truth in other books that have nothing to do with Mani, and Christ handed them down—for so Christ said, that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete himself, would lead into all truth—then, in accordance with Christ's word, I reject the scripture of Mani.

AUGUSTINE said: Since, then, you have been unable to prove how Mani is an apostle of Christ, and you demand that I prove how Christ sent the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, whom he promised, so that you will reject the scriptures of Mani if you find Christ's promise fulfilled apart from the scriptures of Mani—although you ought to have answered my questions first, see, I will answer first all the same and show you when the Holy Spirit whom Christ promised was sent. And he went to the gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.

And when he had taken the book of the gospel, he read aloud: "While they were saying these things, Jesus stood in their midst and said to them: Peace be with you; it is I, do not be afraid." And as he read, he said: This is after the resurrection. And having said this, he read on: "But they were troubled and terrified, and thought they were seeing a spirit. And he said to them: Why are you troubled, and why do such thoughts arise in your hearts? Look at my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet. And while they still did not believe and were marveling for joy, he said: Have you anything here to eat? And they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten in their presence, he took what was left and gave it to them, and said to them: These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled. Then he opened their minds to understand the scriptures, and said to them: Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things. And I will send the promise of my Father upon you; but stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high." And when he had handed back the book of the gospel, he took the Acts of the Apostles and said: We have heard that the holy evangelist recalled Christ's promise, the one found in the Gospel according to John, which Felix here has mentioned. For where the Lord said, "I am sending you the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete," it was John the evangelist who wrote it. But what I have just read, the evangelist Luke attested, and he agreed with the truth of the apostle John. Let us see also how what the Lord promised was accomplished and how it was fulfilled, so that, once the fulfillment of the Lord's promise has been set out from the canonical books of the holy Church, we may not look for another Paraclete, another Holy Spirit, and so fall into the snares of deceivers.

And he read aloud from the Acts of the Apostles: "In the first book, O Theophilus, I gave an account of all that Jesus began to do and to teach, up to the day when he chose the apostles through the Holy Spirit and commanded them to preach the gospel. To them he presented himself alive after his passion by many proofs, appearing to them over forty days, teaching about the kingdom of God, and of how he lived among them. And he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, you have heard from my mouth: for John baptized with water, but you will begin to be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you are also to receive not many days from now, by Pentecost. So when they had come together, they asked him, saying: Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom of Israel? But he said: No one can know the time which the Father has set by his own authority; but you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth. When he had said this, a cloud took him up, and he was carried away from them. And as they were gazing after him as he went into heaven, behold, two men stood by them in white clothing, who said to them: Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven. Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a sabbath day's journey away. And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room where Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James were staying. All of these were persevering with one accord in prayer, with the women and Mary, who had been the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers. And in those days Peter stood up in the midst of those listening and said—there was a crowd of about a hundred and twenty men gathered together—Brothers, this scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold by the mouth of holy David concerning Judas, who was guide to those who arrested Jesus; for he was numbered among us and had his share in this ministry. This man, then, acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and he tied a noose around his own neck, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. And this became known to all who lived in Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood. For it is written in the book of Psalms: Let his homestead become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it; and let another take his office. Therefore, of these men who have gone about with us all the time that the Lord Jesus Christ went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us, one must be a witness with us to his resurrection. And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias. And they prayed and said: You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen to take the place of this ministry and proclamation, from which Judas fell away to go to his own place. And they cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was counted as the twelfth along with the eleven apostles." And when he had read this, he said: We have heard who was ordained in the place of Judas the betrayer, as I mentioned a little earlier, so that no one may creep by fraud into the number of the apostles and deceive the ignorant with the name of apostleship.

Now let us see, as we promised, how Christ's promise concerning the Holy Spirit was fulfilled. And having said this, he read at the passage: "When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them tongues divided as of fire, which rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance. Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, men from every nation under heaven. And when this sound occurred, a crowd gathered and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own speech and in their own tongues. And they were amazed and wondered, saying to one another: Are not all these who are speaking Galileans by birth? And how is it that we recognize in them the language in which we were born? Parthians, Medes and Elamites, and those who dwell in Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs—we heard them speaking in our own tongues the mighty works of God." And when he had read this aloud, he said: Have you now heard of the Holy Spirit and how he was sent? What you demanded of me I have proved; it remains for you to do what you promised. Since we have found when he sent the Holy Spirit whom he promised, reject that scripture which, under the name of the Holy Spirit, sought to deceive reader or hearer.

FELIX said: I do not deny what I said: that when it has been proved to me that the Holy Spirit has taught the truth which I seek, I reject that scripture. For Your Holiness has read me this, where the apostles received the Holy Spirit. And among those very apostles I seek one who will teach me about the beginning, the middle and the end.

AUGUSTINE said: If you read that the Lord said, "I am sending you the Holy Spirit, who will teach you the beginning, the middle and the end," you rightly bind me to show whom the Holy Spirit taught. FELIX said: Since Your Holiness says that the apostles themselves received the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, I say again: let whichever of the apostles you wish teach me what Mani taught me, or refute his teaching—whichever of the twelve you wish.

AUGUSTINE said: Far be it from the faith of the apostles that they should teach the doctrine of the sacrilegious Mani. But since you say that one of them ought to refute the teaching of Mani, and the holy apostles are now no longer in the body, I—the least not only of all the apostles but of all the bishops (for when could I aspire to the merits of the apostles?)—will refute the teaching of Mani, so far as the Lord has deigned to grant me of that same Spirit of his, once we begin to read what follows in that letter which you yourself do not deny to be Mani's.

FELIX said: You said that the apostles have departed from the body; their writings remain in force to this day. And since Your Holiness has spoken, and since you have given us leave to say whatever we wish without any fear: you said, "I refute the law of Mani," and I say: Every man is a liar; God alone is true. It is the scriptures of God that speak.

AUGUSTINE said: You indeed are a man, and, as the facts themselves will presently show, a liar. And since you have said what you wished, not from the scripture of God, I too must say what I wish. For if your Mani has the truth, it cannot be destroyed by me either; if it is falsehood, what does it matter by whom it is destroyed? Yet since you spoke about the writings of the apostles—that although they are not in the body, their writings are here—the apostles were taken up before the error of Mani had come into the world, and that is why no writings of the apostles are found arguing explicitly against Mani. Nevertheless, I will read aloud what the apostle Paul, in that Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, whom he had received, foresaw would come concerning such men as Mani was and as you are, so that you may recognize it. And taking the apostle Paul's letter to Timothy, he read: "Now the Spirit says plainly that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared, forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. If you put these instructions before the brothers, you will be a good minister of Jesus Christ." And as he read, he said: I say that this was pointed out and expressed through the spirit of prophecy about you and about such people as say that some creature of God is unclean and who say that all sexual intercourse, even that with one's wife, is fornication—for that is what he means by "forbidding marriage." But if you deny that all intercourse is fornication, or if you say that all human food which is permitted and granted to people to eat is clean, then you are not one of those whom the apostle foretold and prophesied. But if you are found among those I have described, then here you have the apostle Paul destroying and refuting the teaching of the Mani who was to come. So answer what I ask: Is all intercourse fornication, or is intercourse with one's wife not a sin?

FELIX said: Let what the apostle said be read to me again. And it was read aloud: "Now the Spirit says plainly that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared, forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. If you put these instructions before the brothers, you will be a good minister of Jesus Christ." FELIX said: Mani did not depart from the faith, as Paul says, in the way that others departed from the faith, as it were into a sect of their own. But Mani did not depart from any sect, such that it could be said that he departed from the faith.

AUGUSTINE said: Since I see that you are unwilling to answer what you are asked, lest you be found either not to hold the Holy Spirit, whom we have already proved was sent to the apostles, or not to be among those whom Paul marked out as yet to come—where he prophesied about you yourselves—I will answer briefly. Taking what you said in your own sense—"they will depart from the faith," since only those depart from the faith who were once in some faith, whereas Mani was in no faith from which he could depart, but remained in the one he was in—I ask you this: Has Mani, or rather the doctrine of lying demons that was in Mani, led no Catholic Christians astray so that they departed from the faith? For if many are led astray by you, and through you, and through that doctrine, so that they depart from the faith and give heed to deceiving spirits such as was in Mani, and begin to say that all intercourse is fornication—which is why the apostle says "forbidding marriage"—and begin to say that the meats people eat are not God's creation but the handiwork of demons, and are unclean, then it is plain that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who was in the apostle Paul, foretold concerning these people that they would depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits such as was in Mani. Now, then, since I have answered, it is only fair that you answer what I asked: whether you do not say that all intercourse is fornication. Or if you will not answer this either, answer what I asked first, and prove that Mani is an apostle of Christ. Or if you will not do that either, allow me to refute his teaching, as I promised, while his letter which you call the Letter of the Foundation is read.
FELIX said: And I answer what Your Holiness says: that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, came in Paul.
AUGUSTINE said: Not in him alone.

FELIX said: I am speaking about him, because if he came in him, then he came in all of them. And if he came in him—for Paul says in another letter: "We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect comes, the things that were spoken in part will be done away with"—we heard Paul say this, and then Mani came with his preaching, and we accepted him in accordance with what Christ said: "I am sending you the Holy Spirit." Paul too came, and he himself also said that this one was yet to come; and afterward no one came. That is why we accepted Mani. And because Mani came and by his preaching taught us the beginning, the middle and the end; taught us about the making of the world, why it was made and from what it was made, and who made it; taught us why there is day and why there is night; taught us about the course of the sun and the moon—because we did not hear this in Paul, nor in the writings of the other apostles, we believe this: that he is the Paraclete. And so I say again what I said above: if I hear, in some other scripture where the Paraclete, that is, the Holy Spirit, speaks, about whatever I may wish to ask, and you teach me, I will believe and renounce Mani.

Augustine said: You say that you do not believe the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, was in the apostle Paul, because the apostle Paul said, "For we know in part and we prophesy in part." From this you think that the apostle, with these words, was foretelling that someone else would come after him to preach everything he himself could not, since he spoke only in part; and you believe this man is Mani. First, then, I will show from the apostle's own reading why the apostle said this. Next, since you said that Mani taught you the beginning, the middle and the end, how and why the world was made, the course of the sun and moon, and the other things you mentioned: we do not read in the Gospel that the Lord said, "I am sending you the Paraclete to teach you about the course of the sun and moon." He wanted to make Christians, not astronomers. It is enough for people to know about these things as much as they learned in school, for ordinary human purposes. Christ said that the Paraclete would come to lead into all truth; but he did not say there "the beginning, the middle and the end"; he did not say "the course of the sun and moon." Or, if you think this teaching belongs to that truth which Christ promised through the Holy Spirit, I ask you how many stars there are. If you have received that Spirit you speak of, whose task it is to teach the things that I say do not belong to Christian discipline and doctrine, you must tell me and answer me. For you have made yourself a debtor: if I ask you anything about such matters and you do not answer, then that Spirit of whom it was said, "He will lead into all truth," will not be seen in you, if indeed those things belong to that truth. So choose which you want, and be ready to answer me about these things as a man who has received the Spirit who leads into all truth, and who says that knowing these worldly things belongs to that very truth. I, for my part, can tell you the things that belong to Christian doctrine; but you, who think that how the world was made and what goes on in the world belong to it, must answer me on everything. And plainly, when you answer, you will have to prove it. But before you begin to speak—in case you have something that the man you followed made up—let me first teach what I promised: why the apostle said, "We know in part and we prophesy in part."

He was saying, as the reading itself will soon show, that while a person is in this life he cannot attain everything, but attains only in part in this life; and that the Holy Spirit himself, who teaches in part in this life, will lead us into all truth after this life. To make this perfectly plain, listen to the apostle. And as he said this, he read from the apostle: "But whether there are prophecies, they will pass away; whether there are tongues, they will cease; whether there is knowledge, it will pass away. For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect comes, what is in part will pass away. When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I understood like a child, I thought like a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things. For now we see through a mirror, in a riddle, but then face to face." And when he had read it, he said: Now tell me, if the apostle was foretelling the times of Mani that were to come: do you now see God face to face?

Felix said: I cannot do much against your power, for the episcopal rank has wonderful power, and still less against the emperor's laws. Earlier I asked you, briefly, to teach me what the truth is; and if you teach me what the truth is, it will become clear that what I hold is a lie.

Augustine said: It has become clear that you could not prove Mani to be an apostle of Christ; and I will briefly set out why you could not. You said that you proved Mani to be an apostle of Christ from the fact that Christ promised that the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, would come; and that, since you could not find when the one Christ promised had come, you therefore believed it was Mani himself. But when I proved from the holy, ecclesiastical, canonical Scriptures, as plainly as could be, when the Holy Spirit whom the Lord Christ promised had come, you turned around and said that I ought to show you what he taught and whether he did away with the doctrine of Mani. So when I replied that Mani came in the flesh after the apostles, and that their doctrine had been preached by them before Mani was born, I nevertheless said that one of those very apostles, Paul, through the Holy Spirit who had come upon all the apostles, had even prophesied about this doctrine of yours, since it was to come, and had called it a doctrine of lying demons. There I showed that the things Paul said would be found in that doctrine belong to your profession: namely, the forbidding of marriage—since you say that all intercourse, even with one's wife, is fornication—and abstinence from foods that God created—since I know that you call certain foods unclean, whereas he goes on to say, "Every creature of God is good." When at this point I demanded that you answer, you said that Mani had taught you the beginning, the middle and the end, the course of the sun and moon, and other such things. When I showed that these do not belong to Christian doctrine, you replied that the apostle Paul himself had said that he knows in part and prophesies in part. I said that we cannot know divine things while we are in this life, and that here we see through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face; and I asked you, if you think the apostle Paul said this because Mani was to come and teach what Paul could not, whether it is up to you, who say you have received that very Spirit, to see God now face to face. Since you cannot, it is plain that the apostle Paul was speaking of that life of which John also says, "Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; for we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is." When you heard this, you said you could not prevail against my power. That power is not mine; but if there is any, it was given me to refute errors by him who is the power of all his faithful who trust in him with their whole heart. You also said that episcopal authority frightens you, though you see how peaceably we deal with each other, how calmly we debate, how the people present do you no violence and strike no terror into you, but listen most quietly, as befits Christians. You also said that you fear the emperor's laws. One whom the Holy Spirit filled would not fear this on behalf of the true faith. For the apostle Peter too was afraid at the Lord's passion and denied him three times; but when the Paraclete whom Christ had promised, the Holy Spirit, filled him, he was crucified for the Lord's faith; and he who at first had made a denial out of fear later fulfilled a most glorious passion of confession. So from the very fact that you said you fear the emperor's laws—though it is clear enough from other things as well—it appears that you have not found the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth; for even if you were not afraid, you would be refuted on other grounds.
Felix said: The apostles were afraid too.

Augustine said: They were afraid so as to be careful, not so as to hesitate to declare their faith once they were arrested. You ought to have been afraid earlier, so that we would not find you here; now you are already in the middle of it. Why are you afraid, unless because you have nothing to say? For if you had feared the emperors, you would have kept quiet before. But now, when yesterday you handed a petition to the curator and loudly proclaimed in public that you were ready to be burned along with your books if anything evil was found in them—you who yesterday were demanding the laws as if you were brave—today are you fleeing the truth like a coward?
Felix said: I am not fleeing the truth.

Augustine said: Then tell me whether you see God face to face, as you promised, since you said that the apostle Paul was speaking about you, saying that you would receive so full a truth that we should understand or believe that the apostle had it in part and you have it whole.
Felix said: I am not fleeing the truth; I am seeking the truth. As for your saying that I do not hold it, let it be proved to me from the divine Scriptures. That is what I am asking for now.

Augustine said: First admit that you could not prove Mani to be an apostle of Jesus Christ; and then, as far as I am able, once everything contrary has been rooted out of your heart through my ministry, by the Lord's gift, I will plant in you the knowledge of the truth, which, beginning from faith, leads to God.
Felix said: You are telling me to deny my law and accept another—a better one, at any rate, which is what I am seeking. My answer is that I will not deny my law before I accept another.

Augustine said: But first what is contrary is poured out of a vessel, and only then is it filled with what is good. Or, if you still hesitate to pour it out, defend what you are full of. For, as far as the Lord helps me, I will show you how full of filth and blasphemies the doctrine of Mani is, if you allow that letter to be read whose opening we have already discussed, where you could not prove Mani to be an apostle of Christ. But you are stalling precisely so that the rest will not be read, where your sacrileges are openly exposed. Or, if you allow it, let it be read.

Felix said: I allow it, since you said that everything unclean is poured out and then good things are poured in; that was Your Holiness's saying. To which I reply: no one pours out water unless another has filled it.

Augustine said: See how thoughtlessly you have said this—to put it mildly and not call it madness. I certainly gave you the comparison of a vessel: no one can put anything into a full vessel unless what it was full of is poured out.
Felix said: You spoke of one, and I spoke of two.
Augustine said: If you meant two vessels, do you want us to empty that companion of yours and fill him, so that you can pour out what you have?
Felix said: We both have the same water.

Augustine said: Since you are both full of your water, then, what are we to fill in order to teach you, unless one of you pours out what he has? Or, if it is good and should therefore be kept, so that it may be defended, let that letter be read; let us see whether at least the rest can be defended, since you failed at the very beginning. Or, if you say you did not fail there, prove to us how Mani is an apostle of Christ.
Felix said: Christ said that he would send the Holy Spirit, who would lead into all truth.

Augustine said: If you have him, pay attention to what I asked you a while ago. You said that knowing these worldly things also belongs to his teaching. Tell me: how many stars are there, if you have been led into all this truth?
Felix said: And I say that, if the Paraclete spoke through the apostles, he spoke through Paul too; and I ask Your Holiness to show me the things I have already mentioned.
Augustine said: Admit that you could not show what I asked, and I will show from the Scriptures what belongs to the Christian faith.
Felix said: And I, if you bring me the scriptures of Mani, the five authors I told you of, will prove to you whatever you ask me.

Augustine said: This letter is from those very five authors; we opened its beginning and found written there, "Mani, apostle of Christ Jesus." And I see that you are not explaining that very beginning to me, since you do not prove how Mani is an apostle of Jesus Christ.
Felix said: If I do not prove it in this one, I will prove it in the second.
Augustine said: In which second one?
Felix said: In the Treasure.

Augustine said: This Treasure—which you call by that name precisely to lead the wretched astray—who wrote it? Mani. I do not want you to prove it to me from him, because Mani himself is lying when he says he is what he is not.
Felix said: Then you prove it to me through someone else.
Augustine said: What do you want me to prove to you?
Felix said: That Mani is lying.
Augustine said: Because you cannot prove that Mani tells the truth, must I prove that Mani lied?
Felix said: Why could I not prove it? Have the scriptures I asked for been produced, and I failed to prove it?

Augustine said: But you are asking for the scriptures of Mani, which we do not believe; prove it from elsewhere. I, on the other hand, will prove to you from Mani's own scripture that Mani lied and that Mani blasphemed.
Felix said: Let the books be brought.

Augustine said: Here is the letter of Mani which you call the Foundation. In a building the only beginning is the foundation. If I show that he has made a ruin in the foundation itself, why should we look into the rest of his construction?
Felix said: You say this, claiming to show that there is ruin in it. And I say: give me as many judges as you have too, and I will prove to you that he does not lie.
Augustine said: God forbid, for our sake and for the human race, that you should see as many Manichaeans as you see people here.
Felix said: I said, give me what I asked of you.
Augustine said: Whom, then, do you want me to give you?
Felix said: Whomever you like.
Augustine said: I give you these; if you have better ones, ask for them.
Felix said: How are you giving me these?
Augustine said: Those present, who are listening to us.
Felix said: These people are not on my side.
Augustine said: So you are looking for people who favor you, not the truth?
Felix said: People who will listen to me—and not only to me but to the scripture itself—so that it may be tested whether it speaks the truth or lies.
Augustine said: You see, then, that they are listening. Let us read the rest, since you have acknowledged that this letter is Mani's.
Felix said: I do not deny it.
Augustine said: Then let it be read.

Felix said: I have no judges. And he added: Let its opening be read. And when it was read and they came to the place where the same letter has written: "May invisible peace and the knowledge of the truth be with his holy and dearest brothers, who believe and likewise serve the heavenly commandments; and may the right hand of light protect you and rescue you from every evil attack and from the snare of the world; and may the kindness of the Holy Spirit open the inmost depths of your heart, so that you may see your souls with your own eyes," Felix said: Give me a scripture that refutes these things.

Augustine said: So far we have heard nothing evil, except that Mani dared to call himself an apostle of Christ. For what he has said so far belongs to the plaster coating of his deceit and to the sheep's clothing, in which he first speaks good words to them so that he can bring in evil ones. But let us see what he means to bring in by these words. If he brings in anything evil, these words too will be evil and seductive; but if in what follows he says anything good and true, we shall be bound to accept it. So allow what follows to be read.
Felix said: If, then, you assert that good things are set down first and evil things slipped in afterward, how can I believe you, since you first told me good things?

Augustine said: I have so far called these things neither good nor evil. I said, "We have heard nothing evil so far"; I did not say, "We have now heard something good." The only evil thing I mentioned was that he dared to call himself an apostle of Christ. The words he has spoken will turn out to be evil, in light of what follows, if they bring in something evil; they will be good if they bring in something good. So allow what follows to be read. Why are you afraid?
Felix said: I am not afraid.
Augustine said: Then allow them to be read.
Felix said: Let them be read.

And when it was read and they came to the place where it has written, "His most splendid kingdoms are so founded upon a shining and blessed land that they can never be moved or shaken by anyone," Augustine said: This land he speaks of—where did he get it from? Did he make it, or beget it, or was it equal to him and coeternal with him? I mean this shining and blessed land he speaks of.

Felix said: As it is written, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the earth was invisible and defiled [?] and unformed," I understand it this way: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the earth was"—it seems to me as if there are two earths, just as Mani speaks of two kingdoms.

Augustine said: Since you have cited our Scripture, which you people are in the habit of blaspheming, it falls to me to explain it and to show you that this text is written without blasphemy and in accordance with the truth, and not in accordance with Mani; so that then you, in your turn, may answer what I asked.
Felix said: I will answer.

Augustine said: In the words "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," Scripture briefly summed up what God made. Then, since the earth he had made was not yet visible, before he set it in order and adorned it, Scripture went on to explain what kind of earth God had made—what kind of earth it was of which it had said, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." It is as if, on hearing "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," we were asking what kind of earth, and it added: "But the earth"—that is, the one God had made—"was invisible and unformed." So it did not speak of two earths, but explained what that earth was like. Now, then, answer what I briefly asked: this shining and blessed land that Mani speaks of, upon which the kingdoms of God were founded—was it made by God himself, or begotten of him, or coeternal with him? Answer one of the three, if it is no trouble, without evasion.
Felix said: The scripture interprets itself.

Augustine said: If, then, you know of some passage here where the scripture says that God either begot or made that land, or that it was coeternal with him, open it at the passage you know and read it to me. Felix said: It is not in this scripture but in another. Augustine said: Then I trust that, if there is such a scripture, you remember what it said there. So answer me, since you know that scripture; and if I say it does not read that way, you will refute me. But if I acknowledge that it does, I will argue on the basis of what you yourself answer. So tell me—you who have read it in some book or other where you say this is written—did God make this land, or beget it, or was it coeternal with him?
Felix said: Since Your Holiness has just interpreted your scripture as you wished, and I accepted it, you too must accept whatever I say.
Augustine said: For the moment I will accept your answer to what I asked, if nothing in it troubles me; but if something does trouble me, I will tell you my difficulty so that you may answer it.
Felix said: I did not reply to what you said.

Augustine said: Although you ought first to answer what I asked, I nevertheless went so far as to answer you first. Perhaps it did not trouble you; that is why you did not reply. Perhaps your answer will not trouble me either. So answer what I asked.

Felix said: I will answer. And he added: You asked, then, about that land in which God dwells, whether it was made by him, or he begot it, or it is coeternal with him. And I say that, just as God is eternal and there is nothing made with him, everything is eternal.
Augustine said: So he neither begot it nor made it?
Felix said: No, it is coeternal with him.
Augustine said: But if he had begotten it, it would not be coeternal with him.
Felix said: What is born has an end; what is unborn has no end.
Augustine said: Then whose father was he, or of what was he father—he whom he has just now called Father? For if he had begotten nothing, he could not be a father.
Felix said: But there are other things that he begot.
Augustine said: Are those things he begot, then, not coeternal with him, or are they coeternal too?
Felix said: Whatever God has begotten is coeternal with him.
Augustine said: Then you were wrong when you said above, "Everything that is born has an end."
Felix said: For the moment, since I spoke with reference to the birth of the flesh, I was wrong.
Augustine said: Having confessed your error so modestly, may you be found worthy to understand the truth.
Felix said: May God grant it.

Augustine said: Pay attention, then, so that you may begin to recognize the error of this scripture. If the things God begot are not coeternal with him, then that land which God did not beget is better—the land where all the things God begot dwell, the land you say was not begotten by him.
Felix said: All things are equal to one another—both what he begot and what he did not beget, that is, that land where he dwelt.
Augustine said: What? Is he who begot them equal to all of them, or greater than them?
Felix said: He who begot, those whom he begot, and the place where they are set—all are equal.
Augustine said: Are they, then, of one substance?
Felix said: Of one.
Augustine said: What God the Father is, his sons are too, and so is that land?
Felix said: They are all this one thing.
Augustine said: So he is not the father of this land, but its inhabitant?
Felix said: Yes.

Augustine said: If he neither begot it nor made it, I do not see how it belongs to him except merely by being next to him—as when someone has a good neighbor. And then there will be two things, both unbegotten: the land and the Father.
Felix said: No, there are three: the unbegotten Father, the unbegotten land, and the unbegotten air.
Augustine said: Is all this one substance?
Felix said: One.
Augustine said: And so founded that it can never be moved or shaken by anyone?
Felix said: Moving and shaking are different.
Augustine said: Let them be; but still, were these things such that they could never be moved or shaken by anyone?
Felix said: There is a difference between being moved and being shaken.
Augustine said: That is not what I am asking you about.
Felix said: But that is what you want to pin me down on.
Augustine said: Take "be moved" however you like: could it not be moved?
Felix said: I do not say that it could not be moved; but moving is a different thing.

Augustine said: But what I said was "neither moved nor shaken." I did not say, "It can indeed be moved but cannot be shaken," or, "It can indeed be shaken but cannot be moved." I named both: that it can be neither moved nor shaken.
Felix said: Regarding the two things, there is a difference between being moved and being shaken.

AUGUSTINE said: Let us read on, then, and see whether this god, whose kingdoms were founded on a bright and blessed land that no one could ever move or shake, feared no one, as he ought to have feared no one if his kingdoms were so founded that no one could move or shake them. And he read what follows: "But along one part and side of that illustrious and holy land." And as he read, he asked: "Which side? Right or left?"
FELIX said: I cannot interpret and expound this scripture for you, because that is not in it; it is its own interpreter. I cannot say, in case I fall into sin.

AUGUSTINE said: Then let what follows be read. And as it was read and they came to the place where it says: "But the Father of the most blessed light, knowing that a great ruin and devastation, which would rise out of the darkness, threatened his holy ages, unless he set against it an excellent and glorious deity, mighty in power, by which he might at once overcome and destroy the stock of darkness, so that once it was extinguished perpetual rest might be secured for the inhabitants of the light," Augustine said: Now that open blasphemies have begun, if you think they should be defended, tell me what harm this race of darkness could do to God, whom God seems to have feared, lest great ruin and devastation from the darkness should burst into his kingdoms — especially since he said above that God's kingdoms were so founded that no one could ever move or shake them. What, then, was this race going to do to him? Could it harm him, or could it not? Give one of the two answers.

FELIX said: And I answer: if nothing is opposed to God, as the scripture of Mani said, in that there is another kingdom, for what reason was Christ sent to free us from the snare of this death? Whose is this snare, and whose this death? If there is no adversary opposed to God, why were we baptized? Why the Eucharist, why Christianity, if nothing is opposed to God?

AUGUSTINE said: I see that you do not want to answer what I ask you, and that you ask questions so that I will answer you. I do not refuse to do so, as long as you remember that I answer you when you ask, whereas you refused to answer me when I asked. But since you have asked me, hear the answer to your question. We indeed say that Christ came as a liberator, and we say that we are freed from our sins, because we were not begotten of the substance of God but were made by God through his Word. There is a great difference between what is born of the substance of God and what is made by God and is not of God's substance. Whatever God has made, then, can be mutable; but God himself is not mutable, because works cannot be made equal to their craftsman and founder. But you, who a little earlier, in reply to my question, said that the Father who begot the sons of light there, and the air, and the land itself, and the sons themselves are of one substance and all equal, must tell me how the race of darkness could harm this substance, which is surely incorruptible. For if it could harm it, it was not an incorruptible nature; but if it could not, there was no reason why he should wage battle and send here that deity he speaks of.
FELIX said: I ask for a postponement so that I can answer.
AUGUSTINE said: Until when? Is a break until tomorrow enough?
FELIX said: Give me a break of three days, that is, today, tomorrow and the day after, or until the day after the Lord's day, that is, the day before the Ides of December.
AUGUSTINE said: I see that you have asked for a postponement in order to answer; it is only humane that it be granted to you. But if you cannot answer by the appointed day, what will happen?
FELIX said: I shall be defeated.
AUGUSTINE said: What if you run away?
FELIX said: I shall be guilty before this city, and everywhere, and before my own law.
AUGUSTINE said: No, say this: "If I run away, let me be regarded as though I had anathematized Mani."
FELIX said: I cannot say that.
AUGUSTINE said: Then tell us openly that you are thinking of running away, since no one is holding you.
FELIX said: I am not running away.
AUGUSTINE said: As I see it, you do not want to leave as one defeated; but at least say this: "If I run away, I am defeated."
FELIX said: I have said it.
AUGUSTINE said: And how will it be evident from the record that you have run away?
FELIX said: Order that I stay with whomever I choose.
AUGUSTINE said: Choose for yourself one of these brothers present here who are standing at the railing.
FELIX said: Then with the one who is in the middle.
AUGUSTINE said: As you have chosen, you will be with him until the day.
FELIX said: Yes; and I agree to this.
BONIFACE said: May Christ grant that, if I come back with him, he will be a Christian.
I, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church of Hippo Regius, have signed these proceedings, held in the church before the people.
I, Felix, a Christian and a follower of the law of Mani, have signed these proceedings, held in the church before the people.
BOOK TWO
When the appointed day had come, that is, the day before the Ides of December, the proceedings began as follows in the Church of Peace.

AUGUSTINE, bishop of the Catholic Church of the region of Hippo Regius, said: You remember that when we held our discussion some days ago you asked for a postponement, since you could not answer at the time what I had asked. So if in so ample a span of time — after five days, that is — you have thought of something, answer. For this is what I asked then: if nothing could harm God, why did he wage war with the race you call the race of darkness, a war in which he mingled his own substance — which, as you said when already questioned, is what he himself is — with the nature of demons? But if it could harm him, you do not worship an incorruptible God, such as the truth and the apostolic teaching bear witness to.

FELIX said: From the time I left your holiness, so that I might return on the appointed day to answer your question, whatever you wished to ask, the day has come. And since I have had no scripture in my hands from which I could prepare myself, because they have not been returned to me — for no one goes out to a contest without first having practised, and no litigant can go to law without his documents — so too I cannot answer without my scripture.

AUGUSTINE said: You have spent so many days devising this evasion, which can do nothing to help you, since you have a lost cause and a sacrilegious error and nothing to answer. For it is known to all who were present, whom I see present now as well, that you asked only for a postponement of days, and that when you asked for the postponement you ought also to have asked for the books, if you thought they could help prepare you to answer; and you did not do so. I know that you did ask for the books, though not in order to consult them for your preparation, and that was long before you asked for the postponement; but when you asked for the postponement, you made no mention of having the books returned to you and consulting them so that you could be better prepared.
FELIX said: I ask now that the books be returned to me, and I will come to the contest in two days; and if I am defeated, I will submit to whatever you decide.

AUGUSTINE said: I do not think you are a novice in this wicked sect, as you yourself admit. But that you have nothing to answer, even if you do not admit it, everyone now sees. But since you ask for your books back, which are kept under the public seal, and say that after consulting them you can come prepared in two days, remember what is already established: that you were unable to answer the questions put to you.
But take your books, and say what you want brought out of them for you, so that you can consult it now and answer.

FELIX said: All the scriptures that were taken from me. For this is the Letter of the Foundation, as your holiness well knows, and as I too said, because it contains the beginning, the middle and the end. Let it be read, and let whatever evil is charged against my law be proved. And I will repudiate it if the charges brought against my law are proved.

AUGUSTINE said: Since you acknowledge that this is the letter in which the beginning, middle and end of your doctrine are contained, this beginning — where you say that God fought against the race of darkness and mingled a part of himself, which is what he himself is, with the nature of demons, to be polluted and bound — is so sacrilegious that those who hear it can scarcely bear it. This is the first charge against your sect — whether you call it the beginning, or the middle, or the end, I do not much care; yet you do not deny that this has been read from this letter, which you acknowledge to be Mani's. This is the charge against you; defend it if you can, so that we may move on to other matters. Therefore I ask again: if you worship an incorruptible God, what harm could some hostile race or other, which you invent, do to him? If nothing could harm him, there was no reason why he should mingle a part of himself with the nature of demons; but if it could harm him, you do not worship an incorruptible God.

FELIX said: Mani says that there are two natures, and he is now blamed for saying that there are two, a good and an evil. Christ in the Gospel says that there are two trees: "A good tree never bears bad fruit, and a bad tree never bears good fruit." There you have two natures. Then it is written in the Gospel: "Did you not sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from? An enemy has done this." If this enemy is not alien to God, let it be proved to me; if this enemy belongs to God, what sort of seed did he sow? Again it is written in the Gospel, where Christ says that in the last times he will set his throne in the midst of the world, and will send his angels to the east and the west, the north and the south, and will gather all nations before him and separate them as a shepherd separates the lambs from the goats. And to put it briefly, he will say to the lambs: "Go into the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the beginning of the world." He will say to the goats, who are on the left: "Depart from me, you who have worked iniquity; for you had my name, but you did not do the works; go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels." Who are these who have the name of Christ and are sent into the eternal fire with the devil and his angels, and to which side do they belong, these with whom Christ is not mingled, though they bear his name? For this is what Mani says: that those whom Christ condemns are not his. For the apostle Paul says: "The prudence of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be." This is what Mani says: that what is hostile to God does not belong to God; but if it belongs to God, he made an enemy for himself — and Mani does not say that. Again Paul says: "The god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that they do not behold the brightness of the gospel of Christ, who is the image of God." Paul himself says again: "A goad was given to my flesh, an angel of Satan, who buffets me day and night; for this reason I asked the Lord that it might depart from me. And he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you; for strength is proved in weakness." See what the apostle said, see what the evangelist said. Since Mani asserts this — that the one who made war against God is alien to God, whether because Christ was crucified or because all the apostles were, on account of God's commandment — let your holiness tell me whether this one who crucified them, who is displeased by God's commandment, belongs to God.

AUGUSTINE said: You chose to cite the holy Scriptures, from which you have strayed far from the truth by failing to understand them, as though calling on them to defend your empty talk. Yet among all the things you cited — some as they are truly written, some otherwise than they are written — nowhere could you show that God, wishing to drive back a hostile nature that threatened his kingdoms so that he might have rest, mingled a part of himself, which is what he himself is, with the contrary nature of demons and caused it to be bound and contaminated by them. Yet this is what is charged against you. So, finding nothing to answer, you cited passages of the divine Scriptures where it is said of sinners that they have no part in the blessed life which God gives to the good and faithful, and you wanted these to be taken as two natures, in keeping with the ravings of Mani. But the truth says that all these things that we see and do not see, which have natural existence, were made by God; and that among them the rational creature, itself also made, whether in angels or in human beings, received free will. By this free will, if it chose to serve God, it would have eternal happiness with him according to the will and law of God; but if it refused to be subject to his law and instead used its power to act against his command, it would be subject to the punishment due, according to his justice. This is God's omnipotence in creating all things; this is his justice in requiting sinners. Now, that there is free will, and that therefore each one sins if he wills and does not sin if he does not will, I prove not only from the divine Scriptures, which you do not understand, but also from the words of your Mani himself. For, hemmed in, he sees the power of the truth, against which he had tried to bring in against God another nature that God did not make — not with solid truth but with an empty phantasm. Yet, when it came to confessing the truth about free will, the human nature in which God created him prevailed in him more than the sacrilegious fable he invented for himself.

Hear first, then, about free will from the Lord himself, where he speaks of the two trees which you yourself mentioned. Hear him saying: "Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad." When he says "Either do this or do that," he points to power, not to nature. For no one but God can make a tree; but each person has it in his will either to choose what is good and be a good tree, or to choose what is evil and be a bad tree. This is not because the evils that are chosen have any substance in themselves, but because God created all the things he made in their proper ranks and distinguished them by kinds — heavenly and earthly, immortal and mortal — and created all things good, each in its own kind; and he placed the soul, which has free will, beneath himself and above the rest, so that if it served what is above, it would rule what is below, but if it offended what is above, it would suffer punishment from what is below. So the Lord, in saying "Either do this or do that," showed that what they would do lay in their power, while he himself, as God, was secure and certain in himself, and that if they chose good they would receive its reward, and if they chose evil they would suffer its punishment; but he is always just, whether he rewards or condemns.

Hear now how Mani himself — so perverse, so proud that, by introducing another nature and making it equal to God, he brought God down to his own level — nevertheless confessed that there is free will. In your Treasure, to which you gave that name to deceive people, he certainly speaks as follows, as you yourself know: "But those who through their own negligence have not allowed themselves to be cleansed from the stain of the aforesaid spirits, and have not wholly obeyed the divine commandments, and have been unwilling to keep more fully the law given them by their liberator, and have not governed themselves as was fitting," and so on. You see that in these words free will is confirmed, even by one who did not know what he was saying. For whoever is unwilling to keep the law has it in his power to keep it, if he wills. He did not say "were unable" but "were unwilling." Certainly, when they are unwilling to keep the law, they are not forced by the race of darkness; for if they are forced, they are not unwilling but unable; but if they are unwilling, they are certainly not forced not to do it, but are unwilling by their own will. So this unwillingness, which lies in their own will, is certainly sin, without any compulsion from the race of darkness; acknowledge that this is sin without compulsion from the race of darkness. And from this you see where all faults come from, where the deserts of faults come from, and where the allotments of punishment come from.

You also have this in the apocryphal scriptures, which the Catholic canon does not admit, but which are all the dearer to you the more they are excluded from the Catholic canon. Let me cite something from there too, by whose authority I am not bound, but by which you are refuted. In the Acts written by Leucius, which he writes as though they were acts of the apostles, you have this statement: "For the specious fictions and the feigned display and the compulsion of visible things do not proceed from their own nature, but from that man who became worse through himself by means of seduction." See how he said here both "through himself" and "by means of seduction." For the devil was the seducer of man, not a sinner by nature but a sinner first by will. But because it was in man's power not to consent to the seducer, both "through himself" and "by means of seduction" are stated, so that in the words "through himself" you may understand free will, and in the words "by means of seduction" you may understand the devil — not as the oppressor of one unwilling, but as the tempter of one willing.

Accordingly, since I have answered and, as far as I could, proved that what is written in the holy books about sinners and the righteous pertains not to a difference of natures but to a distinction of merits — and in those merits it is not nature that creates necessity but the will that creates guilt — now you answer what I have already asked: if nothing could harm God, why did he mingle a part of himself, his own substance, what he himself is, with demons, to be polluted and bound — something you could not find in any canonical divine Scripture? But if it could harm him, you do not worship the incorruptible God, of whom the apostle says: "To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, incorruptible, the only God, be honor and glory for ever and ever." He also says: "God dwells in light inaccessible." Do the saints not approach that light, of whom it is written: "Approach him and be enlightened"? Do the saints not approach that light, of whom it is said: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God"? But because no one can approach it except the one to whom God himself grants that he may approach, it is therefore in itself inaccessible. For no one can approach it whom God does not wish to approach; but the one to whom he grants it will approach. How, then, could that race of darkness approach the dwelling of God, where the inaccessible light is, which no one approaches except the one to whom God grants it? Or if it had received from God the gift of approaching, he would not have given it for the purpose of assailing God's kingdom, and he would not be afraid. But if he had not given it such a gift, enabling it to approach, he was secure in his kingdom, dwelling in inaccessible light. What could he have to fear from the race of darkness that he should mingle with it a part of himself, his own substance, what he himself is, to be bound, oppressed and contaminated, where it would not only be held captive in misery but would also be purged in shame? For you say — it is an abomination to hear it, but to confound you and perhaps to save you we cannot keep silent — you say that, in order for the part of God to be purged from there, in the ship of light which you call the sun — doing injury to the creator of the sun and to the sun itself, which you say was made such that so great an obscenity is performed there — you say that God, stationed there, transforms his powers into males to arouse the lusts of the female demons, and transforms them again into females to arouse the lusts of the male demons, so that when they inflame the demons with lust for the forms God has fashioned, the demons' members may be loosened, and so the part of God that had been bound there may escape. So great a disgrace, so great a sacrilege you have dared to believe, and you do not hesitate to preach it. This is the middle of your doctrine. And what is its end? What else but that God could not purge it all? And because he could not, you say he will make it into a kind of covering for the race of darkness, so that what could not be purged, and committed nothing of its own accord, may be condemned there forever. So it comes about that your god — not the true God but a fictitious one, not existing anywhere but imagined in your hearts — mingles a part of himself unhappily, purges it shamefully, and condemns it cruelly. Answer these points, then, and begin with what I said: why did God mingle this part of himself, when nothing could harm him? Or if something could, how is he incorruptible?
FELIX said: You claim that Mani is cruel for saying these things; what do we say about Christ, who said: "Go into the eternal fire"?
Augustine said: He said this to sinners.
Felix said: Why were these sinners not cleansed?
Augustine said: Because they did not want to be.
Felix said: "Because they did not want to be" — is that what you said?
Augustine said: That is what I said: because they did not want to be.

Felix said: Why did they not want to be? Is there anyone who does not want to be cured? Is there anyone who does not want to be cleansed? Is there anyone who does not want to be enlightened? Is there anyone who, because he is sick, does not want to come to health? If what Mani says is cruel, that some part of God which could not cleanse itself is bound in the globe, is this not cruel, that Christ, who said, "I came for the sake of sinners," should now send to eternal fire those who bore his name? But, I suppose, they could not fulfil the commandments. If this is cruel, that is crueller still; if that is crueller, that God could not cleanse them and bound them in the globe, then this too seems crueller, that Christ should send to eternal fire those he could not cleanse. Let your holiness explain this matter of cruelty to me.

Augustine said: If you had either understood what I have already said, or admitted that you understood it — for perhaps, having nothing to say, you have pretended not to understand what is plain — you would not be saying these things. For we have already said, and proved from the divine scriptures, that there is free choice; and that God is the just judge of free choice, the rewarder of the faithful, of those who submit themselves to him and are willing to be healed, but the condemner of the proud and the ungodly. Since, then, he came to heal sinners, he certainly heals those who confess their sins, he heals those who repent. But no one repents when someone else has sinned; yet there is a just and true repentance, which is why the Lord himself says: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. Repentance itself shows that if we happen to sin, it is not the doing of an alien nature but of our own will. For if one person repents when another has sinned, that is not a wise repentance but a mad one. According to you, however, there are no sins at all. For the race of darkness does not sin, because it acts according to its own nature; the nature of light does not sin, because what it does, it is forced to do. So you find no sin for God to condemn, you find no sin that repentance can heal. But if there is repentance, there is also guilt; if there is guilt, there is also will; if there is will in sinning, there is no nature that compels it. But if those who cannot accomplish what they want suffer from some weakness — which is why the apostle says: I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members — it is clear that this has come from the inheritance of Adam's first sin and from bad habit. For even today people form a habit by free will, and once they have formed it they cannot easily overcome it; so they have made it for themselves, by their own doing, that a law dwells in their members against them. But those who conceive the fear of God and by free choice submit themselves to be healed by the best of physicians — as merciful a creator as he is a good healer — are healed through the humility of confession and repentance. The proud, on the other hand, who call themselves righteous, or who say that it is not they who sin but something else that sins in them, some other nature that sins through them, become incurable through that very pride and experience the just judgement of God, who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. It is not unworthy, then, for God to say, "Depart into eternal fire," to those who by free choice rejected his mercy, and to say, "Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom," to those who by free choice accepted his faith, confessed their sins, did penance, were displeased with themselves as they had been, and pleased him as they were made through him. Now answer what I asked — but let me ask you this favour, that we not cause needless delays: if nothing could harm God, why did he send us here? If something could harm him, God is not incorruptible.
Felix said: If nothing could harm God, why did he send his Son here?

Augustine said: See how you always ask questions and will not answer the questions put to you. Hear the answer to what you asked, but remember that you do not answer what I say, while I do answer. Nothing can harm God; but he sent his Son to be clothed with flesh and to appear to human beings, to heal sinners, and to suffer for us in that very flesh which he took from us. For in his own nature he could suffer nothing, since in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. In this nature, since the Word was God, he could suffer nothing. But so that he could suffer for us, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The Word became flesh by taking on flesh, not by being changed into flesh; for he took on humanity without losing divinity. And so the same one is God and the same one is man: in the nature of God equal to the Father, in the nature of man made mortal — among us, for us, from us — remaining what he was, taking on what he was not, in order to set free what he had made, not what he was. Christ's passion, then, came not from need but from mercy. For he gave us an example of patience from what is ours, that is, to man from man, to flesh from flesh; yet he himself was not made worse in that flesh, but the flesh was made better in him. Your god's part, however, took on no flesh — for there was nothing in the race of darkness for which it might suffer — and it came down in order to be held, bound and defiled, and to be cleansed in a way more shameful than it was bound. For I have already spoken of its cleansing. The more unworthy all these things are, the easier they are to understand, since such things do not befall the nature of God. And far be it from a devout and faithful mind to believe such things as you believe of God — of the good God, the true God — not a God you have found, but one you have invented. Answer now: if nothing could harm God, why, according to your empty talk, was that pure substance of his sent here, having taken on no flesh, so that it would suffer in itself, if it was going to suffer anything, and not in a flesh it had not taken on?

Felix said: If God could not be harmed by the opposing side, and Christ could not be harmed by the opposing nature, to what did Christ come, to set it free? For, as you say, he came for our liberation. So we were in captivity. If we were held in captivity, and Christ came for this reason, to free us from captivity, then the one who held us was either a stranger to God or a power of God. If the one who held us was a power of God, why was Christ sent by him who held us? If it lay in his own discretion when he wished to release us, why is Christ crucified? Now it is hidden from no one that Christ was crucified. Why did they crucify him? If it is a power of God, it did us no harm. If it was a power of God, we were not captives in its hands, but rather like ourselves with our own prince, like a son with his parents, not like Romans among barbarians. So, since we had been placed with a power of God, there was no need for God to send his Son, so that it could be said that our liberator had come. If, then, it is clear that we had been placed with a power of God, yet the apostle said: Christ has freed us from the curse of the law, because it is written, Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. For this is what the apostle says. If the one who curses all who hang on a tree is a power of God — for Christ hung on a tree, and so did all his apostles who were condemned for keeping his precept — who, then, is this who curses everyone who hangs on a tree?

Augustine said: Those whom Christ redeemed from the devil were held by the devil through their own consent, and had been placed in his condition by the just judgement of God, because by free choice they had consented to him when he led them astray. Just as it was in man's power to consent to the devil and so be taken captive, so it was in the devil's own power, when he was an angel, to sin and so be changed for the worse. So the angel, a sinner by free choice, persuaded man, who had free choice, to sin; so that the devil, had he not willed it, would not have sinned, and man, had he not willed it, would not have consented. But once man was held by the one to whom he had consented — not because the devil had any power of his own, but because it was God's just judgement to hand over into the devil's power the man who had despised God's power over him and refused to obey his law — since, then, Christ found sinners thus under sin, and sin lies in free choice, finding sinners under sin he redeemed those who confessed from the one who was proud. As for what is set down in the law, Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree — which is why the apostle says, Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree — he is not finding fault with the law but commending the Lord's mercy. For Adam had sinned, and that whole mass and offspring of sin was cursed; but the Lord chose to take flesh from that very mass, so that by taking on mortality, which had come as a punishment, he might undo death, and this came from grace. That is why the law says: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. For death itself hung on the tree, a death that came from the curse. So just as by taking on death he killed death, so by taking on the curse he undid the curse. Hence the apostle also says: knowing that our old self was crucified together with him; for from our old self, that is, from the lot of death that came as the desert of sin, he deigned to take mortal flesh from the Virgin Mary, in which to give us an example both of passion and of resurrection — of passion to strengthen our patience, of resurrection to arouse our hope — so as to show us in the flesh he took from our mortal life two lives, one full of toil, the other blessed: the toilsome one, which we must endure, the blessed one, which we must hope for. We endure the toilsome life as the desert of our sin; but he displayed it in his flesh not as the desert of any iniquity of his, but as the work of his mercy. And so that you may know that the law, which you wanted to find fault with, is good, the apostle Paul himself said in one place: The law came in so that the offence might abound. He still seems to find fault with it; but hear what follows: But where the offence abounded, he says, grace abounded all the more. For the law was given to proud people who credited everything to their own strength, so that, when they could not fulfil the law they had been given, they would be found transgressors, and having become guilty under the law would seek mercy from the law's author. Accordingly, a little later the same apostle says: So the law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. But lest you say that he is speaking of some other commandment, he shows that he is speaking of the one of which he had said a little before, The law came in so that the offence might abound, by immediately putting the question to himself: Did what is good, then, become death to me? By no means; but sin, so that it might be shown to be sin, worked death in me through what is good. For sin was there, but sin did not appear; the law was given to the proud man, he acted against the law, and the sin that was there but had not appeared came to light. And sin, once it appeared, humbled the proud man; the proud man, humbled, became penitent; through penitence he obtained mercy. So you have heard the answer to your question; now answer mine: could the race of darkness do God no harm? Then why did he send his part here to be mingled with and defiled by the nature of demons?
Felix said: If we are in our own free choice, let no one compel anyone; when I want to, I will be a Christian. It lies in our will either to be a Christian or not to be one.

Augustine said: That the will lies in our power is evident, and I have shown it from the divine scriptures; even the man who led you into this error was compelled to say so, though against his will. As for your saying, "Let no one be compelled; when I want to, I will be a Christian" — certainly no one is compelling you; be one when you want to, since you came here of your own will and argued these points of your own will. And woe to the will if it is evil; peace to the will if it is good. For whether it is evil or good, it is will. A crown follows a good will, punishment follows an evil will. God is the judge of wills, but the creator of natures. So if you think you are being compelled to be a Christian, hear from us that you are not being compelled at all. Rather, think over what you hear; weigh it; you are in your own will. Examine like a prudent man, if there is any prudence in you, even merely human, whether what has been said is supported by the truth, and whether you yourself have failed in the defence of your Mani, as it appears; and when you want to, become what you are not yet, and cease to be what you are.

Felix said: Now then, briefly, as your holiness said, so that we do not pile up pages: if it please you — as I asked earlier, this is what I came here for — show me the truth, so that it may become clear that what I hold is not the truth, and you will find me ready to believe.

Augustine said: It is already quite clear that what you hold is not the truth. For far be it from the hearts of those who seek or hold the truth to believe that God, forced by necessity, plunged his own substance into the nature of demons to be bound and defiled; far be it from the faithful to believe that God, to free his substance, turns himself into males before females and into females before males to arouse their lust; far be it from the faithful to believe that God afterwards condemns for ever his own substance, which he himself plunged among the demons. So it is plain that this is not the truth. But since you want the truth to be revealed to you in place of this falsehood, now driven out and refuted, if you are still moved at all to come to know the Catholic faith, you can be instructed from the beginnings of the faith. For devout faith makes a person fit to grasp the unchangeable truth; whoever refuses to begin from this faith will remain outside in his pride and cannot be brought to what he is striving for or where he wants to arrive. But since that falsehood is now plain, anathematize the falsehood, so that you can begin to be fit to know the truth.
Felix said: When it has become clear to me. Since it is not clear to me, since the other has not been shown to me, I cannot anathematize.
Augustine said: Is the error that calls God corruptible to be anathematized, or not?
Felix said: Say it again.
Augustine said: Is the error that calls God corruptible to be anathematized, or not?
Felix said: Let it be inquired whether it says so.
Augustine said: This is what I asked: is whoever calls God corruptible to be anathematized, or not?
Felix said: Whoever calls God corruptible is to be anathematized. Is this what you charge me with?
Augustine said: This is what I am asking.
Felix said: Are you now speaking of a corruptible God, and not of what you said at first, that he gave his part to his adversaries?
Augustine said: For the moment answer what I am asking: is whoever says that God is corruptible to be anathematized, or not?
Felix said: Most certainly.
Augustine said: Is whoever says that the nature and substance of God is corruptible to be anathematized, or not?
Felix said: I did not understand what you said.

Augustine said: I am saying what everyone understands who does not pretend not to understand: whoever says that the nature and substance of God — that is, that very thing which God is, whatever it is — is corruptible, is he to be anathematized, or not?
Felix said: Yes, he is to be anathematized, if it is proved to be true.
Augustine said: I have not yet told you that Mani says the nature of God is corruptible; what I told you is that whoever says this is to be anathematized.
Felix said: And I answered: yes.
Augustine said: Is that part which was mingled with the race of darkness of God's nature, or of some other nature?
Felix said: Of God's.
Augustine said: Is what is of God's nature that which God is, or something else, which is not God?
Felix said: That is so: what is of God is God, as it is also written: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it; for God is light, and in him there is no darkness.

Augustine said: You answered well, that whatever is of God's nature is God, and that God is light and in him there is no darkness; and such a light shone in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it. Let us see, then, whether Mani does not say that part of God was overcome by the darkness, and is even held bound, and even stained and defiled, so that it needs the mercy of a liberator and cleanser.
