If he says these things, then by your own judgement, and by your true admissions, he is to be anathematized, since he says that a part of God and the nature of God, which is God himself, was overcome by the darkness and bound and defiled — something you yourself, speaking according to the gospel, could not say; rather, you spoke the truth, that the light shines in the darkness and the darkness did not overcome it. Mani, therefore, is to be anathematized, for he said that the light was darkened in the darkness and that the darkness overcame it.
Felix said: But whatever is defiled and whatever is held captive is also set free; and we, if we have been defiled, are cleansed.

Augustine said: But this is not rightly said of the nature of God. Of a nature that can be defiled it is rightly said that it is defiled and cleansed; but of one that cannot be defiled, you see what a sacrilege it is to say "it is defiled and cleansed" — especially since you say that a certain part of God has been so defiled that it is bound for ever in the globe of darkness precisely because it could not be cleansed. Whoever does not anathematize this gave a false answer a little earlier when he said that everyone who calls God corruptible is to be anathematized.

Felix said: As to what your holiness said, that the part which did not cleanse itself from the defilement of the race of darkness [?] — Mani says this too, that they are not sent into the kingdom of God. But you assert that they are condemned, whereas Mani says that they are not condemned, but are placed as a guard over that race of darkness.

Augustine said: I am dealing with you about the part that you say is cleansed after being defiled; afterwards, if need be, about the part that is fixed in its globe. For the moment: the part that is cleansed was defiled.
Felix said: What is defiled is also cleansed.
Augustine said: Then is whoever says that the nature of God, the substance of God, and that which God is, can be defiled, bound and polluted by the race of darkness not to be anathematized?
Felix said: From what did Christ cleanse us? From what did he free us?

Augustine said: Christ did not free a part of God, nor the nature of God, but by his mercy freed the creation he had made, which had fallen into sin through free choice. He cleansed the thing that could be defiled, he freed the thing that could be taken captive, he healed the thing that could be weakened. But now we are speaking of God, of the nature of God, of the substance of God, of that which God is: could it be defiled, or could it not?

Felix said: Is our soul, which was defiled, from God? If it is not from God, why was Christ crucified for it? So if it is clear that Christ was crucified for the sake of our soul, it is clear that it is from God, and that it was defiled, and that he cleansed it.

Augustine said: I say that not only the soul but also our body, and all creation, both spiritual and bodily, is from God, because this is what the Catholic faith holds. But what God begot from himself, which is what he himself is, is one thing; what God made is another. What God begot is equal to the Father; what God made, being created, is not equal to its creator. We say that one thing is from God which is better said to be of God, because it is what he himself is — such as the only-begotten Son, such as his Word, through whom all things were made; but we say that other things are from God in the sense that he spoke and they were made, he commanded and they were established. The soul comes from this source: it is among the things God made, not that which God begot from himself. That is why the Word, whom he begot from himself, could not be defiled, cannot be, and never will be. But the soul, which he made to rule the body, so that it might serve what is above it and rule what is below it — that is, serve God and rule the body — was defiled through sin when it despised God's law. And God, showing mercy to what he had made, sent the Son through whom he had made it, and remade it through him. When what did not exist was to be created, it was created through the Word; when what had become depraved was to be remade, a creature was taken from that same source, from the Virgin Mary, so that through what was human it might be shown to human beings both what must be endured and what must be hoped for. And so the nature of the Word, the substance of the only-begotten Son of God, suffered nothing, either from the Jews who persecuted him or from the devil, the evil angel, who pursued him. But because he clothed himself with flesh — clothed himself with something mortal, something capable of suffering, something changeable — in what he put on he suffered whatever he willed, as an example of patience, and he restored it as an example of righteousness. Now tell me about the part of God, which is God: can it be defiled, or not? If it can, God is not unchangeable, and whoever says this is to be anathematized. But if it cannot, you see that Mani is to be anathematized, who says that a part of God, the nature of God, that which God is, came here pure to the race of darkness and was bound and defiled, so that it needs to be released and cleansed.
Felix said: Did you say this of the soul, that it is not from God?
AUGUSTINE said: I did not say that. What I said is that it is from God in the sense that it was made by God, not in the sense that it was born out of God.
FELIX said: You have said of the soul that it is not from God but is God's handiwork, since without God nothing exists. That is what you say, and you will not affirm that the soul is from God.
AUGUSTINE said: It is from God, but made by God.
FELIX said: Whether made, or sent, or given, it is from God. So if it is from God, and it has been polluted, and Christ came to free it from pollution, why do you find fault with Mani?

AUGUSTINE said: Because I say that the soul is not the nature of God. It was made by God, sinned through free will, was polluted by sin, and is set free through repentance by God's mercy. You, on the other hand, say that it is the very nature of God. What God is, God from God, you say was captured and polluted in the race of darkness. And there is a great difference between what God begot out of himself and what he made, not out of himself, but out of nothing. That is, when it did not exist at all, it received from God the gift of existing, that is, of being established.
FELIX said: Then it is a part of God.

AUGUSTINE said: You have already been told that it is not a part of God. Now learn how to understand God as the almighty maker. Everything that comes into being, everything that anyone makes, is made either out of himself, or out of something, or out of nothing. Because a human being is not almighty, he produces a son out of himself, and makes things out of something, as a craftsman makes a chest out of wood or a small vessel out of silver. He could make the vessel, but he could not make the silver; he could make the chest, but he could not make the wood. But to make something out of nothing, out of what does not exist at all, so that it exists: that no human being can do. God, because he is almighty, both begot a Son out of himself, and made the world out of nothing, and formed man out of clay, so that through these three powers he might show that his working is mighty in every respect. What he produced out of himself he should not be said to have made, but to have begotten. As for what he made out of something, as he made man out of earth, he did not make man out of earth in such a way that someone else had made the earth for him to make man from, as [someone else] makes the silver for the silversmith, from which he can make a vessel. No, he himself made both what did not exist, so that it should exist, and also what would come in turn from that which he himself had already created out of nothing. In this way, then, the body, the soul, and the whole of creation are understood to have been made by God, not begotten out of God so as to be what God is. So now perhaps you will choose what to hold and what to reject. Choose which is better. We see many changeable things that are nevertheless good, though changeable, and many mortal things that are nevertheless good, though mortal; but the wholly unchangeable good is God himself. Choose, then, which is better for you to hold: that God is changeable, or that what God made is changeable. For you must say one of the two. If you will not admit that what God made is changeable, it remains for you to say that God himself is changeable. But to cleanse yourself of this sacrilege and this blasphemy, so as not to say that the substance of God is changeable, why do you not grant that God, who truly is and is unchangeable (for he himself said, I am who I am), made all things good, but not equal to himself? Since he himself is unchangeable, it is no wonder if what he made, not being equal to him, is not unchangeable but changeable. That is why it could both sin and be polluted through free will, and be set free through his mercy.

FELIX said: You said that a man makes a son for himself, and there is no difference between father and son. Since Your Holiness has brought this up, I in turn reply that God and the things he makes are equal to him.

AUGUSTINE said: You chose not to understand. When a man produces a son, he is not properly said to make him; he is properly said to beget him. In the same way, I told you, God begot his only Son; he did not make him. What he made is not equal to him; what he begot is equal to him. So choose whether you want to say that God's handiwork is changeable or that God's nature is changeable.
FELIX said: Just as God is unchangeable, so the one he begot is unchangeable; and what he made, if it is of his own nature, does not change.

AUGUSTINE said: But you have already been told that what he made is not of his own nature. He made it out of nothing, because he is almighty. It did not exist, and he made it: not out of himself, not out of some thing that he himself had not made, but out of nothing.

FELIX said: I did not say that. What I said was this: since God is unchangeable, what he begot is unchangeable, and what he made is unchangeable. I did not say what he made it from; I did not ask what he made it from.

AUGUSTINE said: But you have heard from me what you did not ask, so that you might at last stop talking nonsense. Almighty God was able to beget out of himself, to make out of nothing, and to form something out of what he had already made: out of himself, a Son equal to himself; out of nothing, the world and the whole of creation; out of something, man from the earth. This he could do because he is almighty. What is out of himself can never be polluted, just as he himself cannot. But what was made by him, not out of him, can be polluted through free will and cleansed through his mercy, by condemning the sin it committed and acknowledging the one who created it. You, however, said a little while ago that whoever calls a part of God corruptible and defilable must be anathematized. Yet you cannot deny that Mani said that a part of God was seized and polluted in the race of darkness, and it is evident that in these words he blasphemed so badly that perhaps he could not have blasphemed worse. So either anathematize him for saying such things, or you must be anathematized and cast out along with him.
FELIX said: Mani says that a part of God was polluted; and Christ says that the soul was polluted and that he came to free it from pollution.

AUGUSTINE said: But the soul is not a part of God. You have already admitted that Mani said a part of God was polluted. We, however, say that the soul was polluted by its will to sin, but that the soul is not a part of God: it was not begotten out of God, but made by God. The soul is said to be from God, then, in the way that some work of a craftsman is said to be from his craft, or made by him, and yet not begotten out of him as his son is. So since you have already admitted that Mani said a part of God is polluted, and you said some time ago that whoever calls God or his nature corruptible or defilable must be anathematized, you have already anathematized what you will not admit. For when you said that it is polluted and that it is cleansed, by the very word "cleansed" you stated that it is polluted, and you have no way of escape. Both Mani and you have said that a part of God is polluted. So anathematize Mani, or you must be anathematized with Mani.
FELIX said: I did not learn from Mani that a part of God was polluted. I learned from Christ that he came for the sake of the soul, which had been polluted.
AUGUSTINE said: You did not learn from Christ that the soul is a part of God.
FELIX said: I learned from Christ that the soul is from God.

AUGUSTINE said: We too have learned that the soul is from God, but it is not a part of God. The soul is from God as a piece of handiwork is from its craftsman, not out of God as the Son is out of the Father.

FELIX said: We are discussing pollution. If the soul, which is from God, has been polluted and can be cleansed by Christ, who came for its sake, then that part of God of which Mani speaks can also be polluted and be cleansed by the command of God himself.

AUGUSTINE said: There you go again, saying that a polluted part of God is cleansed, when a little while ago you had said that whoever calls it corruptible must be anathematized. Now you say that it could be polluted, and you say that it can be cleansed, which confirms that it could be polluted. We do not say this of a part of God; we say it of the soul, which is from him as his work, not out of him as his offspring. So go back to what you are saying, and note the distinction in what we say: the soul is neither God nor a part of God. But you say that Mani said a part of God is polluted, and by saying that it is cleansed he confirms that it is polluted. It remains, then, that you either anathematize him or, holding these views, be anathematized yourself.
FELIX said: Does the soul that has been defiled by sin belong to God, or not?
AUGUSTINE said: It belongs to him, but it is not a part of him.
FELIX said: That is not what I asked.
AUGUSTINE said: Then what did you ask?
FELIX said: Does it belong to God, or does it not?
AUGUSTINE said: I have already said both that it belongs to him and how it belongs to him.
FELIX said: I am asking whether it is from God.
AUGUSTINE said: From God, not out of God.

FELIX said: If it is no sin to say that it is from God, and was polluted, and that Christ came to free it and did free it from sin, why do we find fault with Mani, who says that a part of God was polluted and is cleansed again?

AUGUSTINE said: Because you have already admitted that Mani said a part of God was polluted, and you say that it is no sin to pour out such blasphemy against God. We, for our part, do say that the soul sinned through free will and is cleansed through repentance by the mercy of its creator, because it is not from God as a part of him or as his offspring, but is from God, or made by God, as his work. The difference between our faith and your faithlessness is plain to all. And so, by your own earlier words, since you granted that whoever calls the nature of God corruptible must be anathematized (and it is plain that both Mani and you say this), then because you refused to anathematize him, you will be anathematized along with him.
After this, when they had argued at length with each other, FELIX said:
Tell me now, what do you want me to do?
AUGUSTINE said: To anathematize Mani, to whom all these great blasphemies belong. But do it only if you do it from the heart, for no one is forcing you against your will.
FELIX said: God sees whether I do it from the heart; a human being cannot see that. But I ask this: that you give me assurance.
AUGUSTINE said: In what way do you want me to give you assurance?
FELIX said: You anathematize first, and then I will anathematize afterward.
AUGUSTINE said: See, I am even writing it with my own hand, for I want you too to write with your own hand.
FELIX said: But anathematize in such a way that you anathematize the very spirit that was in
Mani and spoke these things through him.

Augustine took a sheet of paper and wrote these words: I, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, have already anathematized Mani, his teaching, and the spirit that spoke such abominable blasphemies through him, for it was a seducing spirit, a spirit not of truth but of wicked error. And now I anathematize the aforesaid Mani and his spirit of error.

And when he had given the same sheet to Felix, Felix too wrote these words with his own hand: I, Felix, who had believed in Mani, now anathematize him, his teaching, and the seducing spirit that was in him, which said that God mixed a part of himself with the race of darkness and sets it free in so shameful a way that he transforms his powers into women to confront the male demons, and then again into men to confront the female demons, so that afterward he fastens the remnants of that part of himself forever to the globe of darkness. All these and the other blasphemies of Mani I anathematize.
I, Bishop Augustine, have signed these proceedings, conducted in the church before the people.
I, Felix, have signed these proceedings.
